scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): a policy response that grants our duty to repair human-caused harm, then argues the cause of decline is a poor test for action; two developed examples weighing consequences, controlled prose at about 400 words on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Many species today are disappearing, and people disagree about which ones we should try to save.
One proposed policy is to protect endangered species only when human activity is the cause of their decline.
I understand the appeal of this policy, but I believe it is too narrow, because the value of saving a species rarely depends on the cause of its danger.
First, there is a fair point behind the policy, which is that humans have a special duty to repair their own damage.
When our pollution or hunting drives a species toward extinction, we are clearly responsible for fixing it.
For example, governments that banned harmful chemicals helped several bird species recover from near extinction.
This shows that human-caused harm creates a strong and obvious obligation to act.
Focusing on these cases also lets limited resources be used where our responsibility is clearest.
Repairing our own mistakes is both practical and just.
To this extent, the policy identifies a real priority.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why it is too narrow

sentences.text: Second, however, the cause of a species' decline is a poor reason to decide whether it is worth saving.
A species that disappears through natural change is just as lost as one we harmed directly.
Consider an animal vital to its ecosystem that begins to vanish for reasons we do not fully understand.
Letting it die simply because we did not cause the problem could damage an entire web of life that people depend on.
Such a policy ignores the practical consequences, since healthy ecosystems protect our food, water, and climate.
Refusing to help also treats nature as valuable only when our guilt is involved.
A wiser approach weighs the importance of the species, not only the source of its danger.
In conclusion, humans certainly have a duty to save species they have endangered.
But limiting protection to those cases alone would let valuable species vanish for no good reason.
The better policy is to act wherever a species truly matters, whatever the cause of its decline.
